Michelle Pfeiffer in 𝐁𝐚𝐭𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐬 (𝟏𝟗𝟗𝟐) became one of the most recognizable versions of Catwoman ever put on screen. But creating that look was far more difficult than it appeared. Pfeiffer had actually been obsessed with Catwoman since she was young. When she heard Tim Burton was making 𝐁𝐚𝐭𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐬 (𝟏𝟗𝟗𝟐), she wanted the role, but Annette Bening had already been cast. After Bening became pregnant and had to leave the production, Pfeiffer got her chance.⁣
⁣
She took the role seriously. For months, Pfeiffer trained in kickboxing, karate and weightlifting while also learning to use a 12-foot bullwhip. During one of her early training sessions, she accidentally cut her instructor with the whip. By the time filming began, however, she had become skilled enough to perform much of the whip work herself.⁣
⁣
The hardest part may have been the costume. The latex catsuit was molded closely to Pfeiffer’s body. To get inside, she had to be covered in powder before being squeezed into the suit. Air was then removed to create the skin-tight appearance, and liquid silicone was applied to give it its famous shine. Pfeiffer later described it as the most uncomfortable costume she had ever worn. It was so restrictive that she said she could become lightheaded if it remained sealed for too long. The tight headpiece also made it difficult for her to hear her own voice, causing her to sometimes shout her dialogue until Burton told her to speak more quietly.⁣
⁣
More than 60 latex suits were reportedly made during the six-month production, costing around $1,000 each. Ironically, costumes that were once constantly replaced on set have since become valuable pieces of film history. An original Catwoman costume sold for $12,000 in 2017, another with a screen-matched corset sold for $40,000 in 2023, and a Catwoman costume display sold for $63,000 in 2025.
